title: Progress, Not Products
hook: Claire's groom-quality scores are green and her churn is red, and the gap is a dog hiding under a bed.
counterintuition: Progress is not a functional upgrade. It is a specific movement from a strained state to a better one, and the dimensions a buyer cares about most are often the ones teams never thought to measure.
tryThisNow: Name the last product your team shipped. Write three lines: the practical result it creates, how the buyer appears to others, and how they feel about themselves. If line three is blank, you are missing part of the job.
keyTakeaway: Before any design decision, name the full movement the buyer wants to make: the practical change, the status shift, and the emotional change when it works.

breakdown.fastRead: Claire's dog grooming subscription has perfect quality scores and rising churn. The exit interviews say the same thing: every Friday he hid under the bed. The groom quality was not the job. The job was that the dog's experience, and the owner's guilt about it, had to be bearable. That is the distinction between a product and progress. Progress names a movement from a strained state to a better one, and that movement has functional, social, and emotional layers. When a team tracks only the functional layer, it can build an expertly run service that still fails the hire entirely. The full job includes how the buyer feels about themselves when it works.
breakdown.deepRead:
Progress is more precise than satisfaction. It names a movement from a current circumstance toward a better state. The current state has friction, risk, delay, or discomfort. The better state has a shape the buyer can recognize when it arrives. A buyer may want the form filed, the dog calm, the invoice paid, or the room less humiliating. But behind each of those functional outcomes is usually a social story and an emotional one.

At 10:55 in the morning, in a yoga studio office, Étienne faces a member who is pausing her membership. She has been coming for three years. She says the classes are fine. Then she adds: "It is the one hour where I am not managing anyone's feelings." The functional product was adequate. But she hired the studio for social relief, one hour of not being the caregiver, and the emotional change that comes with that. If Étienne treats her pause as a pricing negotiation, he misses the job entirely.

This is why social and emotional forces are part of the work, not decorations around it. A tool that solves the task while making the buyer feel exposed can still lose. A service that delivers less technical capability but lets the buyer feel capable or relieved can win. The discipline is keeping progress tied to a specific circumstance. If the framing expands into happiness or fulfillment without a concrete before-and-after, it stops guiding any decision. Name the before state, name the better state, and hold both close enough to test.
breakdown.fullRead:
A product is a thing. Progress is a change. That difference sounds abstract until a team tries to explain why a customer chose one answer over another, stayed for three years and then left, or returned the upgraded version of something they loved.

The movement a buyer wants usually has three layers operating at the same time. Functional progress is the visible layer: the dog is calm, the document is filed, the car starts, the dinner is on the table. Social progress is about how the buyer appears to or is positioned among other people: the parent looks responsible, the new employee does not seem lost, the patient does not feel like a burden. Emotional progress is about the internal state that shifts when the answer works: the buyer feels calmer, less exposed, less guilty, more ready, or simply less stuck.

Those layers rarely separate cleanly in a live circumstance. Giulia manages a bookshop with a café. She expanded the café because traffic was up. Transaction size has dropped. When she watches remote workers arrive at nine in the morning and leave at noon, buying two lattes and one book, she realizes they are not buying coffee and literature. They are hiring a third place: a functional workspace, a social signal that they are working-but-not-at-home, and an emotional permission to sit without guilt for three hours. The café expansion did not fail because of pricing. It created a second job that now competes with the first one for the same physical space.

Good product work does not rank those layers too early. It listens for how they combine in the specific circumstance. Devon manages a driving range. Survey data says members want to improve power. Observation shows Friday evening pairs arriving together, staying two hours, hitting the same bucket at a relaxed pace. The job is not power improvement. It is low-stakes outdoor social activity with a physical prop. If Devon invests in premium bays designed for serious training, he optimizes for the stated preference while removing the relaxed environment that makes the social job possible.

The useful test is concreteness. A claim that buyers want confidence is too broad until the team can point to the situation where confidence is absent and describe what would be different if it were present. Confidence before a presentation, after a medical diagnosis, during a first gym session, or in front of a teenager's homework are not the same job. Each has different substitutes, different signals of success, and different design requirements.

This also explains why buyers seem inconsistent. The same person chooses a premium option in one moment and the cheapest option in another. The person did not change. The progress target changed. When a team can see the full three-layer movement clearly, and hold it to a specific before-and-after in a real circumstance, product decisions become less like preference guessing and more like helping a buyer cross a specific gap they have already identified. That gap is the specification. Functional, social, and emotional progress together are the standard.

examples.title: At 9:11 a.m., Claire's quality data is green and her churn dashboard is red

planSpec.stakes: quality scores are high but churn is rising and the exit data points somewhere unexpected
planSpec.requiredBeat: at 9:11am Claire's groom-quality data is green but churn is red; exit interviews say every Friday he hid under the bed, revealing that the emotional progress job, the dog's experience plus the owner's guilt, drove the cancellation

examples.scenario: At 9:11 a.m., Claire opens the monthly dashboard with her prediction sticky note still visible: quality score up, churn stable. Quality is up. Churn is up too. She pulls the exit interview transcripts and reads the same line in different forms: every Friday he hid under the bed, he shook when I picked up his leash, I felt terrible the whole day. The grooms were excellent by every measure the team tracked. She must decide whether to rebuild the service around dog comfort or defend the quality scores.
examples.whatToDo: Add the emotional progress layer to the cancellation review. Track whether the dog's experience of the service, and the owner's feeling about it, meets the same standard as technical groom quality.
examples.whyItMatters: A technically excellent service can fail the emotional dimension of the job entirely. Claire's metrics captured the product. They missed the progress the owner was actually trying to make.

examples.title: Étienne hears the hour that has nothing to do with yoga

planSpec.audience: studio co-owner in pause negotiation with a long-term member
planSpec.stakes: a three-year member is pausing and the reason is not the classes
planSpec.requiredBeat: the member says it is the one hour where I am not managing anyone's feelings, revealing that the functional product was hired for a social progress job: relief from a caregiving role

examples.scenario: "The classes are fine," Valentina says, sitting across from Étienne at 10:55 a.m. with her membership card on the table. "I am just burned out." Étienne is about to offer a discounted pause rate when she adds: "It is the one hour where I am not managing anyone's feelings. Not my kids, not my team, not my mother." Étienne sets the pricing sheet aside. The studio is one of the only hours in Valentina's week that belongs entirely to her, and she needs him to understand that before money enters the room.
examples.whatToDo: Name the social progress job before negotiating on price. Valentina hired the membership for relief from a caregiving role. A discount does not address that job; a different framing of what the hour is for might.
examples.whyItMatters: Three years of attendance built around a social progress job will not be retained by a product improvement. Étienne needs to understand the job before he can offer anything relevant.

examples.title: Giulia traces traffic up and transaction size down to a second job

planSpec.audience: bookshop manager reviewing traffic-up but transaction-size-down after café expansion
planSpec.stakes: the café expansion changed who is hiring the space and for what
planSpec.requiredBeat: remote workers stay 3 hours, buy 2 lattes and 1 book as a cover charge; the café is hired as a third place with a functional workspace job, a social not-home-not-office job, and an emotional acceptable-loitering job; two distinct jobs now compete for the same space

examples.scenario: Giulia reviews the monthly P&L at 4:30 p.m. on a Tuesday. Foot traffic is up 28 percent since the café expansion. Average transaction is down 19 percent. She walks the floor and counts: fourteen people with laptops, three with books, two browsing. A remote worker at table seven has been there since 9 a.m., bought two lattes and one paperback. Giulia needs to decide before next quarter whether the café created a new job for a new buyer, or broke the original job for the old one.
examples.whatToDo: Name both jobs explicitly before making any floor or pricing change. The third-place job and the browse-and-buy job may be incompatible in the same physical space at the same time.
examples.whyItMatters: The café expansion succeeded at creating a new hiring occasion. It also introduced a conflict between two jobs competing for the same resource: space, quiet, and atmosphere. Giulia cannot optimize for both without first naming each.

examples.title: You are Thomas, and you need to name the job before choosing the venue

planSpec.audience: operations manager choosing between hotel conference center and farmhouse through second-person
planSpec.stakes: the real progress job is forcing remote workers to be genuinely present together without the escape hatch of normal work mode
planSpec.requiredBeat: the real progress job is forcing remote workers to be genuinely present together without the escape hatch of normal work mode; the farmhouse wins because it removes the wifi distraction; Thomas needs to name the job before choosing

examples.scenario: You are Thomas. The hotel has fast wifi, breakout rooms, and a catering team. The farmhouse forty minutes outside has slow internet, one long dining table, and nowhere to take a side call. Your budget covers either. Reservations close Friday and you are about to choose. The real progress job for this offsite is not completing the agenda. It is making twelve remote colleagues spend two days genuinely present together, without the escape hatch of a Slack channel pulling someone into a corner. You must decide which space gives that a real chance.
examples.whatToDo: Name the job before evaluating the venue features. If the job is genuine presence, the farmhouse's friction is a feature, not a flaw. Choose against the job, not against the amenities checklist.
examples.whyItMatters: Thomas cannot make a good venue decision by comparing room sizes and catering menus. The right choice depends entirely on which environment creates the conditions for the progress he is actually trying to make.

examples.title: Maja discovers the morning voice job behind the pledge number

planSpec.audience: pledge drive coordinator with 40 percent below-target conversion
planSpec.stakes: the appeal is built around journalism, but the job is something different
planSpec.requiredBeat: donors are not preserving journalism; they are keeping one familiar voice on during morning commutes; functional job is companionship, emotional job is managing start-of-day anxiety; journalism is the category, not the job

examples.scenario: Maja stands at the pledge drive whiteboard at 8:40 a.m. with conversion rates 40 percent below last year's goal. The campaign says: support local journalism. Three listener interviews are pinned to the board. All three say the same thing in different ways: it is what I put on when I am getting ready, it is just on in the background, it is the voice I know. None of them mention journalism. Maja must decide whether to rewrite the appeal around a different story before the drive closes on Friday.
examples.whatToDo: Build the appeal around companionship during the morning transition, not the journalism category. Test whether donors respond to losing the familiar voice rather than losing investigative reporting.
examples.whyItMatters: Journalism is what the station produces. Manageable morning anxiety is what the listeners are hiring the station to reduce. Those are not the same job, and they require a completely different appeal.

examples.title: Devon needs to name the social job before picking the investment

planSpec.audience: sports facility manager deciding between premium bays and short-game area
planSpec.stakes: survey says power improvement; observation says something different
planSpec.requiredBeat: survey says power improvement; observation shows Friday evening pairs arriving together, staying 2 hours; the job is low-stakes outdoor social activity with a physical prop; Devon needs to name the social progress job before choosing the investment

examples.scenario: Devon is weighing two capital requests: automated launch monitors for four premium bays at forty thousand, or a short-game area with casual seating at twenty-two thousand. The member survey says power improvement is the top priority. He walks the range Friday evening and sees something the survey missed: pairs sharing a bucket, staying ninety minutes, rarely checking swing data. He needs to decide whether the survey or the observation answers the right question about what members actually hire the range to do.
examples.whatToDo: Name the social progress job the Friday observation reveals before presenting the request. If members hire the range for low-stakes outdoor social time, the short-game area may serve that job better than launch monitors.
examples.whyItMatters: Survey answers reflect stated preferences in the abstract. Observed behavior reflects the job in action. Devon needs to know which one he is designing for before spending forty thousand dollars.

questions.prompt: A dog grooming subscription has perfect quality scores but rising churn. Exit interviews mention the dog hiding under the bed before each appointment. Which progress dimension did the team fail to track?
choices: The functional dimension: whether the groom was completed on time and to specification.
The emotional dimension: whether the owner felt good about the dog's experience each week.
The social dimension: whether the dog's appearance improved the owner's reputation among neighbors.
questions.explanation: Quality scores track the functional output. The owner's guilt about the dog's visible distress belongs to the emotional progress layer, and that layer was driving cancellation regardless of technical quality.

questions.prompt: A yoga studio member says she attends because it is the one hour where she is not managing anyone's feelings. Which progress dimension should the studio owner address to understand the retention job?
choices: Social: the relief from caregiving obligations that the studio hour provides.
Functional: whether the class format matches her fitness goals and skill level.
Emotional: whether the music and studio temperature create a relaxing physical atmosphere.
questions.explanation: The member named relief from managing other people's needs, which is a social progress job. She is not hiring yoga instruction; she is hiring a structured hour that belongs entirely to her. A discount or class upgrade does not address that job.

questions.prompt: A bookshop expands with a café. Traffic rises but average transaction size falls. Remote workers stay three hours and buy one book as what feels like a cover charge. What does the progress lens reveal?
choices: The café pricing is too low relative to competitor coffee shops in the neighborhood.
The inventory selection is insufficiently curated for the type of customer the café is attracting.
Two distinct jobs, a third-place workspace job and a bookshop browsing job, are now competing for the same physical space.
questions.explanation: Remote workers are hiring the space for a third-place job: functional workspace, social legitimacy for lingering, and emotional permission to not be at home or in a formal office. That job conflicts with the browse-and-buy job for the same resource.

questions.prompt: An operations manager is choosing a company offsite venue. The real goal is getting remote workers genuinely present with each other without the normal work-mode escape hatch. Applying the progress lens, which venue feature matters most?
choices: Environmental conditions that remove the usual escape routes and make genuine presence easier.
Fast wifi and professional breakout rooms that allow parallel work streams during the offsite.
A catering team that handles all logistics so the manager can focus on the agenda.
questions.explanation: When the progress job is genuine presence, friction is a feature. A venue that removes normal-work-mode escape options directly serves the job. Amenities that make it easier to retreat into regular work patterns work against it.

questions.prompt: A radio pledge drive built around 'support local journalism' is 40 percent below its conversion target. Listener interviews say they tune in for a familiar voice during morning routines. Which diagnosis fits the progress lens?
choices: The journalism framing is too highbrow for the station's listener demographic.
The appeal targets the product category, not the emotional job listeners are actually hiring the station to do.
The pledge drive is too early in the season and should be moved to a higher-engagement time of year.
questions.explanation: Listeners are hiring the station to manage morning-routine anxiety through a familiar companionship cue, not to fund investigative reporting. The journalism frame describes what the station produces, not the progress listeners are trying to make.

questions.prompt: A driving range survey says members want power improvement. Friday evening observation shows pairs staying 90 minutes sharing a bucket at a relaxed pace. Which source of evidence is more useful for the investment decision?
choices: The survey, because it directly captures stated member priorities and preferences.
Both equally, combined into a weighted average to determine the most popular feature.
The observation, because it shows what job members are actually hiring the range to do on a specific occasion.
questions.explanation: Survey data reflects abstract stated preferences. Observed behavior reflects the live job in a specific circumstance. The Friday evening pattern reveals a social progress job that a power-improvement investment would fail to serve.

questions.prompt: A buyer chooses a premium option in one situation and the cheapest option in another. A product team labels this inconsistent behavior. What does the progress lens suggest instead?
choices: The buyer's progress target changed between situations, making different options the right hire for each moment.
The buyer has unstable preferences and needs clearer messaging to form consistent product loyalty.
The premium positioning is not clear enough, and the buyer defaults to price when uncertain.
questions.explanation: Buyers are not inconsistent; their progress targets shift by circumstance. The same person hires different options because the functional, social, or emotional job they need done differs in each situation.

questions.prompt: A team wants to improve user confidence. Which version of this progress goal is specific enough to guide a design decision?
choices: Users should feel more confident overall after using the product for 30 days.
Confidence should be a key brand value communicated through the product's visual design and copy.
A first-time user completing their initial setup should feel capable enough to use the product without asking for help.
questions.explanation: Progress goals require a concrete before state, a specific circumstance, and a recognizable better state. Option C names the circumstance, the starting condition, and the target state precisely enough to test and observe.

questions.prompt: A team identifies the functional progress their product creates but leaves the social and emotional dimensions blank. What risk does this introduce?
choices: The team will over-invest in emotional design at the expense of core functional reliability.
The product roadmap will expand too broadly and lose focus on the primary use case.
The product may satisfy the practical task while failing the dimensions of the job that drive retention and recommendation.
questions.explanation: A service can execute the functional task correctly and still fail the hire if the social or emotional layer drives the decision to stay or leave. Claire's grooming subscription is the exact example: perfect functional output, failed emotional job.

reviewCards.front: What are the three layers of progress a buyer may be making at the same time?
reviewCards.back: Functional progress: a practical change in their situation. Social progress: a shift in how they appear to or relate to others. Emotional progress: a change in how they feel about themselves.

reviewCards.front: A product has perfect quality scores and rising churn. What should you examine that the quality metrics cannot show?
reviewCards.back: Examine the social and emotional dimensions of the job. Technical quality tracks the functional output. If the buyer's social or emotional progress is not being served, excellent functional scores will not prevent cancellation.

reviewCards.front: A buyer stays three years and then leaves. Nothing about the product changed. Where does the progress lens direct your investigation?
reviewCards.back: Investigate whether the buyer's circumstance changed such that the job the product was hired to do no longer needs doing, or a different job became primary. Retention loss does not always mean product failure.

reviewCards.front: A team writes 'users want confidence' as a progress goal. What is missing?
reviewCards.back: A concrete before state, a specific circumstance, and a recognizable better state. Confidence in what situation, compared to what starting point, with what observable signal that the progress happened?

reviewCards.front: Survey data says one thing; field observation says another. Which one does the progress lens treat as more reliable?
reviewCards.back: Observation of behavior in a specific circumstance is more reliable than stated preferences in the abstract. Surveys capture what people believe they want; observation captures what job they are actually hiring a product to do.

implementationPlan.title: Writing a Three-Layer Progress Statement
implementationPlan.coreSkill: For any product or service, write a complete three-layer progress statement: the functional movement, the social change, and the emotional shift the buyer experiences when the job is done well. Hold all three against the circumstance before making any design or investment decision.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a product review focuses only on functional metrics, then ask the team to fill in the social and emotional columns before the review closes. If either is blank, pause the decision.
If a wellness tool or habit is not sticking, then write what functional, social, and emotional progress it was supposed to create. Check whether the tool serves all three in the actual moment of use.

If you keep returning to a particular product, place, or routine, then name what three-layer progress it delivers. That clarity helps you find or build better substitutes when the original is unavailable.

If someone's feedback about a product or service surprises you, then ask what state they were in before they used it and what state they expected to be in after. The gap names the progress they were hiring it to make.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, pick one thing you use regularly and write three sentences: what functional problem it solves, how it affects how you appear or relate to others, and how it changes how you feel about yourself. If any sentence is vague, make it concrete before you stop.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, ask someone why they stopped using something they used to rely on. Do not accept the first answer. Probe for the social and emotional layers beneath the functional explanation. The real job is usually in the second or third answer.

memorableLines.text: A product is a thing. Progress is a change.
memorableLines.why: It states the core distinction in six words, making it easy to retrieve and hard to misremember.

memorableLines.text: The full job includes how the buyer feels about themselves when it works.
memorableLines.why: It extends the job definition beyond functional output and names the emotional layer as a design requirement, not an afterthought.

memorableLines.text: That gap is the specification. Functional, social, and emotional progress together are the standard.
memorableLines.why: It closes the chapter's argument by naming all three layers as the measurement standard, replacing a purely functional design target.
